title: Virtual Memory
summary: Each process sees its own address space, backed by RAM and disk as needed.
what: Virtual memory is the illusion that every process owns a large, private, contiguous address space. The hardware translates VA → PA through page tables and a TLB. The OS fills the illusion: demand paging, copy-on-write, file-backed maps, swap.
why: Isolation, convenient linking (every process can start at the same VA), and overcommit. It is also why 'out of memory' and 'page fault' are different sentences.
mental: A library card catalog. Your card names a shelf that might be in the reading room (RAM) or in off-site storage (disk). The clerk (page fault handler) fetches as needed.
points: Translation is the always-on part. Swap is optional.
Demand paging: a freshly mmap'd file is not all in RAM.
COW fork: parent and child share frames marked read-only; a write faults and copies.
The working set must fit or you thrash.
mistakes: Thinking a page fault is always a bug

interview.q: Is swap required for virtual memory?
interview.a: No. Translation and isolation work without swap. Swap is a way to overcommit RAM.
Parent and child share physical pages marked read-only. A write triggers a fault; the OS copies the page and resumes.

title: Indexes
summary: Auxiliary structures (usually B+ trees) that make predicates cheap at the cost of writes and space.
what: An index is a data structure maintained with a table so a predicate (equality, range) can find rows without a full scan. Clustered indexes are the table; secondary indexes point at keys or row ids. Hash indexes help equality, not ranges.
why: The difference between 10 ms and 10 s. Also the difference between a fast write and a slow one: every index is extra work on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.
mental: The card catalog, not the shelves. You still have to maintain both when a book moves.
points: B+ tree: ranges and ordered scans. The default.
Selectivity: an index on 'gender' is often useless; an index on 'email' is not.
Covering: if the index has every column you need, you never touch the heap.
Write amplification: each extra index is another structure to update.
mistakes: Prefix wildcards (LIKE '%foo') that cannot use a B-tree

interview.q: Why does an index slow writes?
interview.a: Each insert/update/delete must maintain the index structure (splits, leaf writes) in the same transaction.
A composite index (a,b,c) supports predicates on a, a+b, a+b+c — not b alone.

title: Round Robin
summary: Time slices in a cycle. The quantum is the whole design.
what: Ready threads sit in a FIFO. Each runs for at most one quantum, then is preempted to the tail. Fair in the sense of equal CPU over a long window; response time depends on n × quantum.
why: It is the first preemptive scheduler people implement, and the quantum question is a real engineering knob (too small: context-switch tax; too large: FCFS in disguise).
mental: A talking stick with a kitchen timer.
points: Quantum q. n runnable threads → a thread waits about (n-1)q between slices.
I/O-bound threads often yield before q; they look snappy.
CPU-bound threads are sliced; they need other policies (priority, CFS vruntime) for fairness in work, not just time.
usage: Cooperative thread pools with a time slice
mistakes: q = 1ms on a machine whose switch costs 0.3ms
Calling RR 'optimal' — it is not SJF

interview.a: Response time looks good until context-switch overhead dominates utilization.
RR is preemptive FCFS with a cap. Long jobs cannot convoy the CPU for their whole burst.

title: Mutex
summary: Mutual exclusion: at most one holder. The lock you actually want most of the time.
what: A mutex is a lock with ownership: acquire, enter the critical section, release. Only the owner should unlock. Implementations: TAS/CAS spinlocks (short), futexes (spin then sleep), adaptive mutexes.
why: Race conditions are 'you needed a mutex' (or a lock-free protocol you can prove). Deadlocks are 'you needed an order on mutexes'.
mental: A bathroom key. One holder. Don't copy the key (unlock from the other thread). Don't wait in the bathroom for a second key (lock order).
points: Protect data, not code. The invariant lives on the data.
Hold time is the scalability limit. Do not I/O under a lock.
Lock ordering prevents deadlock. Document the order.
Try-lock and timed lock exist; they are not a substitute for a design.

code.title: The shape, not the API

mistakes: Locking too coarse (one big mutex) or too fine (deadlock soup)
Forgetting the data is still racy if you read it without the lock 'because I only read'

interview.a: A mutex has ownership and is binary. A semaphore is a counter: it can permit N and is often used for signaling, not just exclusion.
A busy-wait burns a core. Spin briefly if the critical section is tiny and the holder is on another core; then sleep (futex).
